facts: Counting my early browser-based use of Claude and ChatGPT to obtain code snippets, I started using AI for programming more than two years before the original interview.
I consider my way of obtaining AI support at work to be continually evolving because the technology changes rapidly.
About a year before the original interview I tried to stop using the IDE and instead use AI in the terminal.
At the original interview I generally prompted AI directly in the terminal to generate nearly all my code. I rarely touched the code myself and estimated AI generated 95–98% of it.
I previously used IDE-integrated AI but stopped because I found it too slow. I recalled Cursor being at the forefront of code suggestions about two years earlier.

I found IDE autocomplete suggestions based on page context and explicit prompts often missed the target. I now rarely use an IDE and prefer terminal prompts. I predicted IDEs might feel outdated within a year; this was my opinion at the time.

My AI-supported workflow changes rapidly and would have been different two months earlier. Currently I give a ticket from a project manager or product owner and the relevant code to AI, ask it to research and make a plan, and have it save the plan to a file so the plan survives a crash or interruption.
I read the saved implementation plan to assess whether it solves the task, then reference the file to instruct AI to execute a particular part, write tests or implement a feature.
I rated AI use very often across all listed programming activities because I no longer generally assume a task is beyond AI's ability.
I use AI for every programming task and, when it struggles, consider how to change my prompt or plan.
I confirmed my very-often AI-use rating for all activities in the table.
I was working on two tasks at once rather than just one; I offered the interviewer a choice of recent programming examples, including a conventional small service task.
For the conventional service task, I told the team at stand-up that I had finished my previous task. The project owner sent me a ticket about an endpoint receiving failed cloud-test results.

The ticket concerned an endpoint that received failed cloud-test results but showed only the test name, not the test bucket. I needed to add the bucket so results could be sorted by it, although I initially did not know what the bucket meant. I identified the referenced [PROJECT] repository, cloned it locally and started the AI tool I called cloud code.

For the test-bucket task I launched Claude Code via a restricted initializer with settings limiting file access to protect passwords. I gave it the ticket and repository, asked it to devise a solution and save it to a file. It read the code, requested permissions and proposed a plan with bucket examples. I carefully read the plan and gained a vague understanding of buckets but still lacked the business context, partly because I had worked there only one month.

For the test-bucket task I asked an experienced developer to review Claude's plan and explain the context, both to understand the system and to show interest in colleagues' perspectives. He approved the approach, explained where tests run and why bucket names matter, and showed me examples in the database. I then asked Claude to execute the plan. I found the automated tests were already failing before implementation, so I discarded the first solution, returned to baseline, asked AI to fix the ex

For the test-bucket feature, asking AI to implement it twice was faster than saving and restoring the first solution because it was small. The final pull request had one change fixing the automated tests and another implementing the feature.
I did not manually write any code for the test-bucket feature; I drank coffee and watched AI do the work, joking about waiting for the world to end.
In my general work I generate code every day, often through AI rather than manually. I use AI very often for code writing.
I do a fair amount of code reviewing in my work, but was considering how to rate its frequency.
I rated code reviewing as sometimes in the general work-activity discussion.
Our workplace has automated AI review for pull requests: when someone creates a pull request, AI reviews it first and generates comments.
When I review a pull request, AI has already left comments. I read the pull request and its comments, including every AI-generated comment, so I consider this a form of AI use.
In code review AI assists me rather than doing all the work, unlike my heavy AI use for generating, refactoring or debugging code. I rated reviewing code sometimes.
I rated debugging very often in my general work, alongside code writing.
I see writing code and debugging as two sides of the same coin.
I rated testing very often, though the amount varies by project. I think AI is particularly good at generating tests, for example producing twenty tests quickly.
I wish I did testing even more frequently than I already do.
I specify every task before working on it, including debugging and new features, especially with AI. I rate specification very often and use AI for it very often.

I enjoy documenting things and taking meeting notes, but AI has changed my perceived need for documentation: it can explain how code works, so I have become more forgiving about skipping written documentation. I feel I should document daily and use AI for documentation only sometimes.
For general work, regardless of AI use, I rate documentation often and think my colleagues would agree.

I rate continuous learning often and definitely use AI for it. Previously I learned through tutorials and reading; now I prefer describing a small project in a browser and having AI guide me through it.
Of the development activities I perform very often, writing code takes the most time overall.
I distinguish three categories of AI coding work. For critical services at work that must not break, I use AI to generate code if needed and then read it very carefully.

For critical professional services I make sure I understand every line before review, asking AI for explanations or rewriting code myself if needed. I think this may be somewhat excessive but distinguish deliberate agentic coding from the negatively perceived practice of shipping unreviewed vibe-coded work.

In critical work I accept AI-generated code only after reading and understanding it sufficiently to stand behind it. For my hobby website for a dance association, I have a clear goal and use AI to implement it, merge the code without reading it and test functionality instead. I see this as closer to vibe coding but still goal-directed agentic coding.

For my dance-association website I test the feature I asked AI to implement, although I may miss breakage elsewhere. I accept that risk because a failed dance-course purchase is less serious and can be caught and corrected. I have experimented with letting AI work very quickly, and have been surprised that things do not break.

By ordering changes carefully and testing them, I built a dance-association website that I said generated 400,000 in online sales over four months (currency unspecified). I said it works without breaking despite my not reviewing its code.

For the third category, my boss asked me to build a tool at work without code review and as fast as possible to explore what could be accomplished. I used the same approach of ordering careful incremental steps from AI, but quickly.
I am trying to improve at using sub-agents, where one agent starts several other agents and agents monitor each other, to work faster. I do not consider myself proficient at this yet.
I very often work with code I did not write or parts of the code base I am unfamiliar with.

Examples of working with unfamiliar code include reviewing pull requests and the task I referred to as the hooks task, where AI helped me understand code, the feature and implementation. I work with a lot of unfamiliar code.
I feel I am becoming good at using AI to understand unfamiliar code and identify a small atomic change that I can be confident does not break surrounding functionality.
For another AI-assisted task I recalled the workflow of obtaining a product-owner ticket and giving it to AI, and introduced an earlier example involving a ticket-fetching tool.

An earlier ticket contained alternating text and images. It was clear to a human but cumbersome to transfer and explain to AI, which I run on another server rather than my own machine. I asked AI to create a tool to fetch tickets directly and speed up that workflow.

Manually transferring a ticket's text and images to the AI server could take about fifteen minutes, so I used AI to create a tool that fetches the ticket description and images by ID in one command. A second command asks AI to understand and solve it. I optimized the input workflow with AI before solving the actual ticket.

I now use my AI-built ticket-fetching tool for every ticket: it gathers the description, images and all comments into one file, which I ask AI to read and solve. I said this lets the project owner give me five tickets rather than one, which I can fetch and work on across different screens.
Around four years before the interview I solved many analogous tasks myself, but then had to weigh the time invested against the benefit.

I estimate that manually building a comparable ticket-fetching tool would easily have taken a day, whereas with AI I can do it in about ten to fifteen minutes. This is an estimate, not a measured comparison.

When building small scripts manually for unfamiliar APIs, figuring out how to structure the script could easily take an hour. I have made many such scripts before. Now I can try AI first, and if it fails, try a different approach or copy and paste instead.

I feel AI allows more adventurous experimentation because it uses AI resources rather than as much of my time. Previously I might choose a ten-minute manual task over four hours building and then maintaining automation. I also contrasted colleagues [COLLEAGUE 1] and [COLLEAGUE 2], who can concentrate silently on difficult problems for hours, with myself, for whom that is not a strength.

I think my strengths are more interpersonal or human-oriented, and I can get into tasks quickly but need breaks from long, difficult tasks; my mind wants to walk or read news. I contrasted myself with colleagues who can sustain extended focus.
I feel AI levels the playing field for me by preserving a plan and allowing me to ask where we left off and what the next step is, without needing to maintain uninterrupted focus for four hours.
Ideally I read and understand AI-generated code, but sometimes it produces code whose form or readability makes me question whether it is acceptable.

For professional projects I ask AI to refactor unreadable generated code, or take a different approach, rather than accept arbitrary output. For hobby projects I may accept code directly and test the feature. I prefer a concrete validation case suited to the project and problem.
I like reproducing the specific problem locally, using Git for version control so I can roll back, applying the fix and testing whether it works.
I consider choosing the best way to validate a fix a skill in itself and noted that automated testing is a common approach.

I consider myself more pragmatic than [COLLEAGUE 1], who strongly prioritizes automated testing and application stability. I may consider cutting corners if business needs do not allow another eight hours writing and running tests, while my colleague prioritizes the application regardless of business pressure. I regard that rigor as part of what makes him an extraordinary programmer.
I mentioned a tool redacted as [AI ASSISTANT], which was new to me and which I had not investigated deeply, as an example of a potentially always-running AI assistant.
I am interested in always-running AI assistants on a computer that can start other AI agents to solve tasks; I see this as moving the human layer of abstraction further back.

I suggested researching how developers prepare for the next rapid wave of AI change: what resources they consult and how they think and work. I used a provocative metaphor that developers who still type all their own code could become obsolete soon; this was my prediction, not an observed outcome.
I continued my joking prediction about manual coders becoming obsolete and said I do not have a good answer to how to keep up with the next AI developments, but find the question very interesting.
I suggested exploring where developers read about AI, how they think and experiment, and whether they experiment at work or home.
